This is about a developer who spends a lot of time looking into how websites are put together. The old way was slow: open DevTools, click through a few elements, copy colors, check font sizes, scan media queries, and write it all down somewhere.
That process eventually became a Chrome extension.
Design System Extractor reads the visual system of the page open in the current tab and packages the results into a ZIP. Version 1.4.0 is now on the Chrome Web Store.
Using it is simple: open a page you're allowed to inspect, run the extension, and press Capture.

The extension scans the page's DOM and styles for colors, typography, spacing, border radius, shadows, breakpoints, motion, contrast pairs, and interaction states. It also finds familiar components like buttons, inputs, cards, and badges.

Before downloading, you can review what was captured and drop anything you don't need. The ZIP contains JSON tokens, CSS custom properties, a Tailwind theme, Style Dictionary files, and a list of components found on the page.

What turned out to be hard was the screenshots. Things get different with fixed headers, lazy-loaded sections, nested scroll areas, or endless feeds, so the extension gave up on a single full-page capture. Instead, it finds usable sections, scrolls them into view, and crops each one separately. The cropped images can be reviewed one by one before export. Infinite scroll is handled this way too: the capture has a defined stopping point instead of scrolling down forever.

Page data processing happens entirely on your own computer, inside the extension. There's no backend and no analytics service. The developer receives no page addresses, no extracted styles, no screenshots, and no usage logs. Temporary viewport images stay in memory only while component crops are being made. Form input values, passwords, cookies, auth tokens, and browser storage are never touched at all.

Since this is the first public version, the developer is especially looking for reports of pages where the capture misses a section, crops it oddly, or pulls out the wrong tokens. Cases like that decide what gets fixed next.

Dependencies usually get added once and forgotten. They do their job, tests pass, and nobody looks again. Meanwhile the web platform has kept moving, and a good share of the libraries still sitting in package.json now live inside the browser.

blocks.cap: A git diff showing npm dependencies removed from package.json, marked in red.

blocks.x: In a mid-sized JavaScript app, dependencies that the platform now handles on its own add up to roughly 60KB to 90KB after compression: date and number formatting, HTTP requests, modals, tooltips, deep cloning, grouping arrays. The libraries stick around because npm audit checks security but rarely asks 'can the browser already do this?'

Baseline, from the WebDX Community Group, reports how safe a feature is across Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari. Limited availability means it hasn't landed in every engine yet; Newly available means it just landed everywhere; Widely available means it has held that status for 30 months. That 30-month window becomes the baseline for the audit.
Before removing anything, ask three questions: is it safe for users, what does replacing it cost, and does the platform feature actually cover the real use case.

The internationalization bundle is the easiest case. timeago.js, pluralize, numeral, and humanize-duration can move to Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, PluralRules, NumberFormat, and DurationFormat. Using all four saves 14KB gzipped. Intl.DurationFormat is still Newly available, though, so check your user base first.

HTTP calls call for more caution. axios is 17KB gzipped and superagent is 19KB, but for ordinary requests, fetch with AbortController is enough. Fetch, however, doesn't reject on 404 or 500, and has no interceptors, automatic retries, or upload progress. If you need even one of those, build a thin wrapper yourself.

blocks.cap: A Bundlephobia screen showing axios at 44kb minified and 16.6kb gzipped.

blocks.x: UI basics give the cleanest results. A single dialog element removes both a modal library and focus-trap, and locking background scroll takes one line: body:has(dialog:modal){overflow:hidden}. Dropdowns and tooltips are covered by the Popover API and CSS anchor positioning. This bundle alone saves around 24KB gzipped.

This isn't an argument to rip out all of Lodash, just to stop shipping the parts the browser already has. groupBy becomes Object.groupBy, cloneDeep becomes structuredClone, and set operations move to the native Set methods. debounce and throttle stay, since there's no replacement.

Temporal, by contrast, reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 but isn't in a shipped Safari release, so it isn't Baseline yet. The official polyfill is 44KB gzipped, while dayjs is 3KB. Switching now would add 41KB to the bundle. Until Safari ships it, dayjs stays.

The audit process is short: run npm ls --omit=dev --depth=0 to list shipped dependencies, weigh them with a bundle analyzer, and check the Baseline status of the replacement features on webstatus.dev or MDN badges. It isn't a one-time cleanup but a habit to repeat once a quarter.

Stafford Beer said “the purpose of a system is what it does.” If that holds, one purpose of the information systems we use is to scatter our thoughts, lose them, and let them sit unattended. Writing and organizing tools collect a tax of confused, vanished, duplicated, and abandoned drafts, and users are left with no tool to undo it.

blocks.cap: A sketch by Stafford Beer overlaying the human nervous system onto the viable system model.

blocks.x: The problem, as the author sees it, is that apps lack the ability to change themselves to match our goals. Cybernetics comes from the Greek kybernḗtēs, meaning one who steers a ship, and it deals with systems that endure and adapt within an environment. It has nothing to do with cyborgs or cyberspace.

The core idea is the viable system. It handles its internal state and responds to outside pressure, and losing either ability means losing viability. Here, variety means the number of things something can do. A subway turnstile has only two states, locked and unlocked, but the variety of a person or an organization is uncountable.

A viable system requires a two-layer structure. One is recursion: just as a company splits into divisions, divisions into departments, and departments into teams, a viable system contains viable systems within it. The other is the system–metasystem structure, where instead of crushing things with commands, the inside is left to coordinate itself while a separate system watches progress against goals and adjusts.

This structure maps directly onto a text app's screen. Each rectangle on screen is a widget, and each widget is System 1. Coordinating how multiple text widgets divide up space is System 2, and creating and closing widgets in response to user input is System 3. Today's apps mostly stop here.

What's missing is System 4 and System 5. System 4 watches the environment—here, the text the user is writing—and changes how System 3 behaves. It enlarges and draws attention to passages with a high “variety coefficient,” where meaning shifts depending on how a sentence is broken; it expands orphaned fragments referenced nowhere else to full screen; and it compares against past documents and structure to recommend merging text with high déjà vu.

System 5 watches whether System 4 is doing its job. It tracks whether users actually edit the enlarged widgets, whether they finish writing more often, and whether orphans and duplicates decrease. If something isn't working, it adjusts or notifies the user. The idea that a system's purpose is what it does comes back here: if a system claims purpose X but is observed doing Y and nothing changes, its purpose is Y.

What the author warns against is a tool that claims to know what good writing is. A computer should only handle things with clear answers, like how many words are in a sentence; it can show that a sentence is long enough to confuse, but it shouldn't tell you how to fix it. As Ted Nelson pointed out, today's software uses the computer's capacity for connection to imitate paper. These features should seep into the interface the way a messy pile on a desk signals disorder—not pop up in front like Clippy, but behave like real paper.

blocks.cap: ChatGPT voice mode running on an iPhone.

blocks.x: AI assistants like ChatGPT have gotten better with every new model in capability, accuracy, and response speed. Generative AI still isn't perfect, and it isn't a source you should trust without question, but for people already used to it, switching to voice conversation is more convenient than typing everything out. The early Voice Mode from 2023 ran by stitching together three systems: converting speech to text, having a language model generate an answer, and having a speech-synthesis model read it aloud.

The Advanced Voice Mode that followed handled everything with a single multimodal model, which was a big jump in how it felt. ChatGPT's voice conversations are now handled by GPT-Live, and the naturalness has gone up another level. OpenAI describes it as a “full duplex” structure that listens and speaks at the same time. This is where the earlier voice model's problem gets fixed—the one where it mistook a brief pause for the end of speech and started answering before the person had finished talking.

Now ChatGPT can slip in short acknowledgments like “mm” or “yeah” while a person is still talking. For questions that need reasoning or research, GPT-Live hands the work off behind the scenes to a model like GPT-5.5.

GPT-Live is used in the ChatGPT apps for Android and iOS, and on the web in a browser. ChatGPT Pro, Plus, and Go users get the GPT-Live-1 model, while the free tier gets GPT-Live-1 mini. GPT-Live has pushed aside the older turn-based Advanced Voice to become the default. You start it by tapping the waveform-shaped ChatGPT Voice icon at the far right of the input box. The first time, you'll be asked for microphone permission.

blocks.cap: The ChatGPT Voice settings screen.

blocks.x: Entering voice mode brings up an orb on screen that reacts to you. You just talk as usual. The settings icon at the top right lets you pick the model's intelligence level from Instant, Medium, or High. GPT-Live-1 mini doesn't have this setting, so it requires a paid plan. ChatGPT Voice keeps running even if you switch to another app or lock your device.

GPT-Live still doesn't support screen sharing or video sharing, though. You can go back to the older voice model by choosing a different model under Voice in settings. From the same place, you can change the voice and language, or set ChatGPT Voice to open by default when you launch the app.

blocks.cap: The ChatGPT app icon on an iPhone home screen.

blocks.x: The author, who prefers typing, wasn't especially interested in the new voice mode at first—not until having a few long conversations with it. What stood out wasn't how smart it was, but how quickly it became easy to forget you were talking to an AI. It doesn't interrupt you, and you don't have to wait awkwardly for it to finish. When a question runs long, it almost feels like it senses what you're about to say next.

Because it responds so quickly, it's also usable for real-time interpretation. Scrolling down during a conversation brings up a transcript of what was said. For questions better served visually, it builds and displays an interactive widget alongside its spoken answer.

The default intelligence level is Instant. It favors fast responses while still handling everyday questions without trouble, and hands off searches or deep reasoning to a stronger model behind the scenes without breaking the conversation. For anyone who deals with complex topics often, Medium and High take a beat or two longer to think, but that delay doesn't disrupt the flow of conversation.

blocks.cap: Image courtesy of Square Enix.

blocks.x: Keeping sketches and drafts may be the only proof left that a human made something.
The controversy now facing Square Enix, the Japanese publisher behind Final Fantasy and Kingdom Hearts, is the kind that anyone who makes a living creating things should pay attention to.

As a sister outlet reported, the cover art for the Kingdom Hearts collection, coming to the Switch 2 and other platforms, drew suspicion of being AI-generated within hours of its reveal. The evidence stands out: Donald Duck has three fingers on one hand and four on the other. The watch's details don't line up, the keychains are inconsistent in size, and the whole thing looks sloppy.
Square Enix said it wasn't AI. According to its statement, the image was made by the development team without generative tools, and the errors were human mistakes.

That may well be true. The problem is that no one outside the studio has any way to verify it. Even after the cover was revised three times, fixing some errors while leaving others, the doubt remained. The real story is that uncertainty, and it's bigger than one publisher's cover art problem.
“A human made this” is no longer a sentence that companies or freelancers get to say and simply be believed. It has to be shown. A long-held assumption has flipped.

For decades, people assumed their own work was theirs by default. Why would anyone think otherwise? Now it's the reverse. If a piece of work has even a hint of so-called AI tells, the burden of explanation falls on the person who made it, and “trust me” no longer works.

The fortunate part is that keeping a record of process was already a good habit before any of this. Sketches, rough cuts, contact sheets, and early drafts have always had value—proof of range and skill that the finished piece alone can't show, and promotional material to use later. One reason people respond so well to this kind of content on social media is that it offers clues and texture they can't get anywhere else.

It also benefits the person doing the work. Writing down why a decision was made, whether as a caption or just a private note to yourself, sharpens the decision itself. Half of a sketchbook lives in writing that never gets shared. This isn't new advice. What's new is the size of what's at stake.

Keeping process records used to be a bonus for whenever there was spare time and energy. By the late 2020s, it has become close to essential for any work that could be mistaken for machine-made. Files with live layers, time-stamped drafts, reference boards, even screen recordings of work taking shape—all of it may be needed someday to prove you made it.

So don't throw away rough drafts, keep version history turned on, screen-record when the software allows it, and hold on to files even when it seems you'll never need them again. Suspicion of being machine-made costs clients, work, and reputation, even when it isn't true.
The Gnomon Workshop released Design Mechs in VR Using Substance 3D Modeler. It's a free guide to a VR sculpting workflow, recorded by WB Games concept artist Andre-Lang Huynh.
It's a 30-minute video course covering Substance 3D Modeler and KeyShot.

In the course, Huynh shows his entire workflow for designing and sculpting a mech from scratch using Adobe's VR sculpting software, Substance 3D Modeler. He starts from simple geometric shapes, locking down proportion and silhouette first, then builds up complexity with secondary and tertiary forms like joints and armor plating, plus color and surface detail.
The Substance 3D Modeler features covered include primitives, sculpting brushes, booleans, layers, materials, stamps, symmetry, angle snapping, and reusable kitbash elements.

Once sculpting is done, he moves into KeyShot to apply materials, set up simple lighting, and produce presentation renders. The project files that come with the workshop include the finished Substance 3D Modeler scene.
Andre-Lang Huynh is an advanced concept artist at WB Games Montréal. He designed characters, props, and vehicles on Gotham Knights, including the Batmobile and the Batcycle.

Design Mechs in VR Using Substance 3D Modeler is available through a subscription to The Gnomon Workshop, which includes more than 300 tutorials. The subscription costs $57 a month or $499 a year, with a free trial available.

blocks.cap: An alien made entirely with a Three.js shader.

blocks.x: This cute alien, visualized by Senior Developer Drin, looks 3D but isn't. It was built with Three.js, and what creates the 3D feel isn't geometry but shader math.

There's no mesh, no texture, and not a single vertex behind it. There's only math running inside the shader. The scene consists of one full-screen quad, and each pixel is calculated in the fragment shader by ray marching a signed distance field.

In the end, shader math handles depth, shape, and form on a flat surface. Technically it's a completely flat plane, but it produces the illusion of volume. Ray marching and SDFs are techniques technical artists use to create stylized, geometry-free visuals straight on the GPU.

There's more than one way to build convincing fake 3D. One example is how the director of the Blender short Dust of the Simulacrum solved wide-angle lens distortion. The logo made for Web Entangled Prophecy came out of Unreal Engine 5 using a retainer box and HLSL.

On the Three.js side, there's Chiro Visuals' real-time snowfall system, Yong Su's port of Evan Wallace's WebGL demo into Three.js, and Dan Greenheck's Three.js Water Pro. For the alien setup, click through the link to try it out directly, changing the colors as you go.

blocks.cap: ArtStation and Sketchfab join the KitBash3D and Greyscalegorilla family. Image: KitBash.

blocks.x: ArtStation is still one of the largest digital art communities online. It has more than 10 million registered users. With thousands of digital artists using it as their main portfolio site, it's understandable that news of yet another change of ownership wouldn't sit easily.

Epic Games, maker of Fortnite and Unreal Engine, announced it is selling ArtStation and the 3D asset site Sketchfab. Both were acquired five years ago, in 2021. The new owner is KitBash, which runs the 3D asset platform KitBash3D and Greyscalegorilla.

With this deal, Epic will focus on Unreal Engine 6, Fortnite, the Epic Games Store, and its developer ecosystem. KitBash gains a bundle of platforms spanning education, portfolios, and artist discovery all the way through production-ready 3D assets, materials, and publishing.

KitBash sees the acquisition as a chance to build a broader ecosystem covering the whole creative process, from training through publishing. KitBash3D already holds a vast library of production-ready 3D assets and environments, while Greyscalegorilla has focused on materials, plugins, and tools for 3D artists and motion designers.

KitBash co-CEO Banks Boutté said: “These are platforms where people have built portfolios, careers, and communities. That trust is real, and our first priority is protecting what users value most on each platform, listening to the people who rely on them, and building the future carefully.”

ArtStation was founded in 2014 by Leonard Teo and Kevin Strike as a portfolio hub for digital artists in games, film, and entertainment. There were concerns when Epic acquired it in 2021 too, but joining the ecosystem benefited many artists, and Epic also lowered marketplace fees. Bill Clifford, SVP overseeing the Unreal ecosystem at Epic Games, said “KitBash will expand opportunities for artists to connect with each other and showcase their work in new ways at every stage of the creative process.”

The new owner says nothing changes for artists right away. Existing portfolios, libraries, and workflows carry over as is. KitBash3D and Cargo customers also keep their kits, assets, and subscriptions. Intellectual property stays with the artists, and KitBash has stated firmly that it will protect ownership, attribution, and creative rights. Subscription prices and access terms stay the same too, and 2D/3D asset and print sales continue uninterrupted. Neither announcement, however, mentions any change of ownership for Fab, Epic's digital asset marketplace.

Over the long run, how the expanded ecosystem will fit together remains to be seen. Some artists are optimistic that the consolidation will widen exposure, while others worry about concentrated ownership and reduced competition between platforms.

The biggest expectation is that ArtStation's AI policy will change along with its ownership. Many feel KitBash's first task should be cutting down the AI slop that has piled up on both platforms. For those who have left ArtStation in recent years, that alone is the reason to come back. ArtStation wrote on X that it is listening to artists' voices, saying “there's trust to earn, a lot to learn, and important work ahead.”

AI tools like Figma Make have been shortening design cycles by taking over repetitive, mechanical work that used to tie up teams. But few teams actually know how much time they've saved, or where the gains are biggest. Figma's data science team set out to find an answer, but common methods like A/B testing or causal inference couldn't capture the full complexity of AI.

To put the result first: design work done with Figma Make was 20% faster and 16% easier. PMs benefited the most, with their tasks 23% faster and 37% easier. These numbers come from a randomized controlled trial in which 100 participants solved the same tasks with and without Make.

Measurement is tricky because of confounding variables. Tenure, experience, and task difficulty all affect how fast someone works. Everyday statistical methods can't strip out these variables, which makes it impossible to tell how much of a productivity change is actually due to AI.

blocks.cap: Comparing the trade-offs of online A/B testing, causal inference from observational data, and randomized controlled trials.

blocks.x: One approach worth considering is giving one group Make and turning it off for another. In theory, confounding variables scatter randomly, but there's no way to control whether the two groups end up doing equally complex tasks. Causal inference from log data was also a dead end. Propensity score matching (PSM) only works if every confounding variable is captured in the logs, and an anonymized user ID doesn't reveal a person's subjective design experience. There were no usable instrumental variables (IV) in the logs either.

The option left was a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Random assignment spreads confounding variables evenly across both groups, having everyone solve the same tasks removes differences in task properties, and a trained research team coordinating the sessions reduces variance. Sample size was set by running a power analysis using effect sizes from prior industry research like the GitHub Copilot RCT: 50 product designers and 50 product managers, 100 people in all.

blocks.cap: Task 1. Convert a design that starts in light mode into dark mode.

blocks.x: The tasks had to be something anyone would recognize, regardless of experience, so the team settled on editing a social media post. They built three scenarios: changing UI and appearance, building a new screen from a base design, and adding interactions and responsiveness. The hardest part was finding a point that wasn't too easy for product designers but not too hard for PMs. The tasks went through three redesigns after internal pilots. Since differences in how sessions were run were themselves a confounding variable, the team built a script and troubleshooting guide for every facilitator to follow.

blocks.cap: Completion time down 20%, task ease up 16%, perceived Figma usability up 15%.

blocks.x: All 100 participants completed the study. Cumulative task completion time dropped 20%, task ease rose 16%, and perceived Figma usability rose 15%. PMs improved by a wider margin than product designers on every measure. Under an interaction regression model, PMs using Make recovered 23% cumulatively, and across the full experiment they performed at an efficiency nearly matching product designers who didn't use Make.

Where the gains showed up differed by role. PMs reported improvement on the two easiest, fastest tasks but showed no statistically significant improvement on the hardest, longest task. Product designers showed the opposite pattern, with significant time improvement only on the hardest task. For designers, Make works as a tool that accelerates zero-to-one and complex interaction design; for PMs, it's more of a basic tool that lets them pitch in on design quickly.

The analysis combined hypothesis testing with OLS regression models, and any result not noted otherwise is statistically significant. The design gives confidence that Make caused these improvements. Figma is preparing a similar RCT around its new design agent.

When building a web interface that feels tactile, bouncy, and breakable, the usual industry choice is a physics engine. Matter.js, Cannon.js, or hand-rolled WebGL have become standard for immersive gamified sites.

The Isadora Agency team hit the same fork in the road while building Stress Release, a digital stress-relief toy that lets burned-out creatives hit, stretch, and distort animated UI characters. While looking at physics engines, they found a decisive difference: “A physics engine creates plausible motion. In our case, we needed motion the animator had intended.”

blocks.cap: A character card. It shows the personality and visual identity that define the animation sequence and interaction states.

blocks.x: What they needed wasn't realistic simulation but frame-specified response. So they dropped physics engines entirely and built the experience with programmatic control of Lottie state, DOM manipulation, and distance-based math.

The core requirement was fully deterministic control. The .json Lottie files the animators built demanded frame-level sequencing. The “mega squeeze” reaction, for instance, needed an exact 181-frame build-up followed by a release sequence. Handling state through Lottie's native API let them trigger animations precisely without overwriting the keyframes the animators had carefully crafted.

blocks.cap: Lottie responses tied to distance-based click detection create the sensation of actually hitting the character.

blocks.x: The Lottie runtime renders JSON vector animation internally as SVG. Elements are selected by ID and CSS class, while behavior is driven by Lottie segments, CSS transforms, and click-event math. Every click is measured against the character's center point: page coordinates are converted to the character's local coordinates, then distance is found with the Pythagorean theorem.

That one number decides score, feedback intensity, and explosion position all at once. Within 10 pixels of the center scores 100 points, within 40 pixels scores 70 to 90, and beyond 145 pixels scores 0. It resembles a dartboard with concentric scoring rings. The explosion Lottie is repositioned to match the click coordinates.

Desktop clicks and mobile taps are both captured with native event listeners. Without adding a raycasting layer, the interaction model never drifts out of sync with the animation rendering. Each character stores idle, squeeze1 through 3, and ending animations as frame ranges, and every click plays the next segment before returning to the idle loop.

Building on the DOM eliminated the need to re-measure bounding boxes on every device. Responsive resizing is handled entirely through CSS variables, and the Lottie SVG scales naturally without losing state.

Lottie JSON is heavy. With 21 character animations plus explosion variants layered on top, keeping performance intact, especially on mobile, took real effort. performance.now() measures initial load time, and anything over 5 seconds gets flagged as a slow connection. Instead of loading all 21 at once, they're loaded two at a time in sequence with await so lower-end devices don't choke. Heavy explosion animations are destroyed and recreated on the fly to keep idle-state memory down. On the shelf screen, where all 21 run at once, quality is lowered to 0.5 and speed to 0.6; on the play screen, which focuses on a single character, quality stays at 1.

blocks.cap: The “mega squeeze” state. Layered animation sequences, background transitions, and timed feedback build up the sense of impact.

blocks.x: Design requirements decide the technology. Because they needed customized, controlled visual responses, they chose programmatic state control over emergent simulation. The code only listens, calculates, and pulls the trigger — the feel was set by the animator.

This week brought a stir over phrases like “massive fines” and “sweeping new AI regulation.” Looked at closely, it's much narrower and more commonsense. The goal is to make AI visible where it should be visible, and the target is specifically AI-generated content.

Starting August 2, 2026, AI labeling becomes a legal requirement for companies serving EU citizens. Like the European Accessibility Act, this isn't just a problem for EU companies. Any company anywhere is covered if people inside the EU use its AI output.

The point of labeling is to make it clearly recognizable to everyone that content was artificially created or manipulated. Article 50(4) of the AI Act names four targets: deepfakes that look like real people, objects, places, or events and could be mistaken for genuine ones; chatbots and AI agents, which must disclose that they are not human; fully AI-written text on matters of public interest that hasn't gone through human review; and emotion-recognition and biometric-categorization tools.
Both the provider that builds or supplies the AI and the deployer that uses it carry the obligation. As with GDPR or the EAA, licensing an outside tool doesn't let you dodge Article 50.

Most other AI-assisted work falls outside the new transparency rules. If a human reviewed and edited the output, and a named individual or organization takes editorial responsibility, there's no disclosure requirement. Small edits like spelling, grammar, formatting, cropping, color correction, or AI translation don't count as generation. Summarizing, synthesizing images, substantially rewriting, and adding or removing elements from a photo, on the other hand, do count.
“A human glanced at it” doesn't qualify as editorial review. The Commission made clear that review must be substantive and that a responsible person must be named.

blocks.cap: Sparkle icons are everywhere across AI products, but they don't tell you which content was actually AI-made

blocks.x: The sticking point is the icon. As part of its code of practice, the Commission issued an EU AI icon set. It's an “AI” mark similar to the AI label in the Carbon design system, not the sparkle icon many products use. Sparkles are used more often to mean “this has an AI feature” than “this content was made by AI,” making them ambiguous — exactly the kind of signal the rule is trying to filter out.

blocks.cap: The EU's official AI icon set — three versions: basic AI, fully generated, and partially modified

blocks.x: The Commission made clear that using the icon alone doesn't automatically mean you're complying with the law. A barely visible icon, text buried in the footer, or a label that flashes for a second and disappears all fail. The icon has to be clearly visible, carry a plain-language label, and be readable by assistive technology. It's safer to place plain text like “AI-generated” next to the icon, and the label has to travel along when the content is reshared or downloaded.

blocks.cap: Research showing a sparkle alone struggles to signal that something is AI-generated

blocks.x: This isn't just an EU matter. China made labeling and watermark metadata mandatory starting September 1, 2025. California's SB 942, after being amended by AB 853, took effect on the same date as the EU, August 2, 2026. South Korea's AI Basic Act took effect January 22, 2026, and is considered the first comprehensive national-level law to mandate deepfake labeling; fines run around $20,000 per violation, with a one-year grace period before enforcement. India applies amended IT rules starting February 20, 2026, requiring disclosure of “synthetically generated information.”
If AI content could be mistaken for something human-made, whoever made it has to say so clearly, and the UI has to flag the parts that AI made. That's the core of the rule. It helps weed out AI slop.
Starting today, you can build skills for the Figma agent directly inside the product. Skills you create can be posted to the community to share with others.

A skill is ultimately a markdown text file. With its shape of ordered instructions or prompts, it looks at first like an engineer's tool, but it actually fits well for carrying the judgment and taste designers bring to their work.

blocks.cap: Illustration of interface elements — arrows, letters, smiling faces, flowers, and squares — strung along a striped path

blocks.x: The author got a feel for it while building a motion tutorial. They wrote a skill that applies their go-to easing curve to whatever keyframe is being worked on, named it /ease-like-miggi, and when the team used it, the team's motion started moving like their own.

Here's how it's done. You give the agent a design frame as reference, or tell it the steps and guidelines you want, and ask it to build a skill. Once a draft appears, you preview it and try it right away in chat. As you use it, you adjust steps, change the format, or open the markdown editor to refine it by hand. Many also work alongside the Figma MCP server in third-party agents.

blocks.cap: Mockup of AI work prompts surrounding a mobile design canvas

blocks.x: A few of the ten the community picked. /xray-scan turns a photo or description into something like an X-ray — black and white with glowing edges that becomes a collage when several are layered (Adele Ix). /find-animation-opportunities flags spots that should move but are static, and spots that shouldn't move but are, and even suggests the numbers (Emil Kowalski, Linear). /camera-pan-and-zoom builds a camera rig without touching the frames to stage pans, zooms, and rolls (Mallory Dean, Figma).

/better-interface hands the agent a personal rulebook spanning typography, layout, accessibility, motion, and product copy (Jakub Krehel, Interfere). /component-handoff picks a single component and unfolds it into a documentation frame — from a header with name, version, and owner, to a live preview, variant grid, dos and don'ts, state breakdown, and full anatomy (Mauro Berteri, Itti Digital).

blocks.cap: A sliding-button component spec laying out wait, drag, loading, and done states alongside a spec table

blocks.x: /create-color maps visible fills, strokes, and shadows to tokens or styles and catches hardcoded colors. For gradients, it notes each stop's position, color, and linked variable (Ian Guisard, Uber). /analyze-components scans a page to flag orphaned components, duplicates, and naming errors, and swaps instances all at once (Amy Ha, Walmart).

/ui-state-expander takes a single screen and expands it into loading, empty, error, disabled, partial-data, and edge-case states, attaching triggers, copy, transitions, and implementation notes (Linda Ojo, Paystack). /superfuture-design-review sorts review results into red for blockers, yellow for recommended fixes, and green for what already works (Joey Primiani). /usability-test-guide attaches guiding questions next to frames to build a usability-test guide (Neha Kodi).

PTC has released the FeatureScript MCP Server for Onshape. It lets you build your own CAD features using natural language and AI.
Released as part of Onshape Labs, it works like this: describe the feature you want in words, and AI builds it in FeatureScript, tests it, debugs it, and refines it until it behaves as intended.

blocks.cap: Onshape Labs FeatureScript MCP

blocks.x: Companies automate repetitive work, build tools tailored to their workflow, and preserve engineering knowledge in the process.

For example, a feature built by feeding AI a PDF containing a standard's definitions can apply a complex helix with a single click. A tool for wire shelving or sink racks takes user-set parameters and generates grid patterns and support structures. In effect, you build a dedicated button for the bottleneck that always slowed you down.

“FeatureScript is the abstraction language we use to build our own features, and we've open-sourced the whole thing. You can build missing functionality, add what you need, and some customers were already doing exactly that. Our intent is to let people adapt the CAD system to their own needs,” Darren Henry, PTC's General Manager and Senior Vice President of Onshape, said in an early preview given to DEVELOP3D.

“As everyone knows, AI likes coding. With Onshape, you get a solid set of standard tools and extend from there to fit your own needs. Solid standard CAD tailored exactly to what you need — that's where we think Onshape's strength lies.”
The FeatureScript MCP Server also extends reach to coding LLMs like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini. Built on the Model Context Protocol, it connects AI directly to FeatureScript code.

Asking AI to write a FeatureScript feature has been possible for years. The difference now is that it also tests and evaluates. “It writes the code, tests it, evaluates the output, and rewrites it if needed. It judges for itself whether the result matches the goal, and does all of this autonomously,” explained Cody Armstrong, Onshape's Senior Director of AI Innovation.

What Onshape is especially counting on is persistent memory. “It writes down what interactions it had in the past, on its own, into memory. The goal is to avoid making the same mistake again,” Armstrong said. By writing and reading notes on past errors and solutions, the agent gets better over time.

It's not limited to building features within CAD itself. Working with external LLMs, it also builds prompts that construct standards-compliant CAD models. In a shell-and-tube heat exchanger case, a 267-part assembly was completed without a person drawing a single sketch line. A cut list was included, along with several tables such as a welding specification sheet.
Whether it's images, PDFs, standards, or internal guidelines, the more you provide, the better the initial results. Still, a feature can be built from a single simple prompt.

“The future of AI in CAD isn't simple text-to-CAD, it's text-to-code-to-CAD,” said David Katzman, PTC's EVP and General Manager of Onshape and Arena. “The real value of AI lies in turning a validated idea into a tool you can rewrite again and again. With the new FeatureScript MCP Server, Onshape has become the most rewritable production CAD there is.”
Marmoset has released version 5.03, the latest update to Toolbag, its real-time rendering and lookdev software for games, VFX, and portfolio work.
It's another sizable free update. New Text and Scatter layers have been added, along with support for IES light profiles, physical light units, and 3Dconnexion's SpaceMouse input devices.

Toolbag is a tool for handling lookdev, compositing, and final rendering with a light footprint. Game artists use it heavily, but its use is growing in other fields too. You can quickly check an imported model while dialing in PBR materials and lighting, and since Toolbag 4.0 in 2021, it has also supported 3D texture painting. You can bake texture maps and pass them to other DCC tools or game engines, or render stills and animation directly inside it.

Two new texture layers arrive with 5.03. The Text layer projects lettering onto a model or aligns it along a mesh surface, with controls for font style, letter spacing, and alignment. The Scatter layer scatters elements like rocks or leaves across a specific surface, or distributes them by projecting from 2D, 3D, or decal planes.

On the performance side, you can now pause or disable UDIM tiles individually, and layer caching has been added, making the average project “about 2.7x” faster. Importing vector designs like logos or labels as SVG is also now supported.

Lighting changed in two ways aimed at reproducing real light more accurately. It now supports IES profiles that capture the actual falloff pattern of real light fixtures, which you can get free online. You can also specify brightness in physical units, which makes a particularly noticeable difference in interior scenes. Motion blur can be previewed in the viewport, and procedural skies gained Sun Scale and Sky Color controls.

Baking now lets you set a maximum ray distance, and curvature map quality has improved, especially near UV seams. Multiple material selection is also supported. Viewport navigation now works with 3Dconnexion's SpaceMouse line.

Toolbag 5.03 runs on Windows 10 and macOS 13.5 or later, and supports AMD, Apple Silicon, and NVIDIA GPUs. Perpetual licenses are $399 for individual artists and $1,299 for studios. Subscriptions are $18.99 a month for individuals and $49.99 a month for studios.
